system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2129-08-18 16:01:00 to 2129-08-19 17:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis and recent Puestow procedure was readmitted for worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He reported a syncopal episode possibly related to pain, initially concerning for seizure but determined to be a pseudoseizure. CT imaging showed expected post-surgical changes without abscess, mild colonic wall thickening of uncertain significance, and a trace pericardial effusion. He was managed medically with IV pain control and antiemetics, advanced to a regular diet, and remained stable. Wound cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus and Group B Streptococcus, interpreted as skin flora without evidence of infection. He improved clinically and was discharged home with oral pain medication and follow-up plans. No surgical intervention was required.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I passed out in the bathroom this morning. I was having really bad stomach pain, like sharp and shooting down to my left testicle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how long has the pain been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About two weeks. It’s been getting worse. I haven’t been able to keep any food down for three days. I’ve been vomiting everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you noticed anything unusual in the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… little specks of blood and something that looked like soot. I was really scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Did you have any other symptoms with the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had chest tightness for the past few days too—like a squeezing feeling. And I’ve been dizzy, nauseous, and sweating a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you said you passed out—how many times has that happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A few times over the last couple weeks. Always when the pain gets really bad. My wife says I go stiff and then just collapse, but I come back quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re going to run some tests to figure out what’s going on. Given your history of pancreatitis, this could be another flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. But this feels worse. And the passing out is new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your blood work now. In the ER, your heart rate was very high—150—and your lactate was elevated, which suggests your body was under stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was concerning, but after fluids, your lactate came down to normal. That’s a good sign. We also did a chest X-ray—no pneumonia or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and did three troponin tests—all normal. So no heart attack. The chest pain is likely related to the abdominal issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the passing out? Is that from the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. When pain is severe, it can trigger a vagal response—your heart slows, blood pressure drops, and you faint. We’re monitoring your heart rhythm to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had seizures before, or maybe they were pseudoseizures. My doctors weren’t sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history mentions that. But during your stay, we haven’t seen any seizure activity on the monitor. These episodes seem more like pain-related fainting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The pain is unbearable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started IV fluids and pain medication. You’re also getting anti-nausea medicine. For now, we’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess tomorrow. If your pain improves and you can tolerate food, we might discharge you the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look better. Your lipase is normal, which is good—it means no active pancreatitis flare. Your lactate is now normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history and symptoms, we think this is an acute flare on top of chronic pancreatitis. Even though lipase is low, your pain and vomiting fit the pattern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on clear liquids. If you keep that down, we’ll advance your diet. We’re also switching your pain meds to oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? I usually take metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held metformin while you were NPO and gave insulin instead. You can restart metformin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? I take Cymbalta, gabapentin, Geodon…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping those for now. Cymbalta and gabapentin can worsen nausea, and Geodon isn’t needed in this setting. Your psychiatrist will help restart if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from metoclopramide to ondansetron—Zofran. It works better for nausea like yours and doesn’t have the same side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well today. You kept down apple juice and broth, and your pain is much better. We think you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel so much better. I’m glad I don’t have to stay longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home with pain meds, omeprazole, and your pancreatic enzymes. Take the Zofran only if nausea returns. And follow up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll make sure to take it easy and eat small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if you have severe pain, vomiting, or pass out again, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have the tools to manage it better. You’re being discharged home today with instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I feel lucky it wasn’t my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all signs point to this being related to your chronic abdominal condition. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, and pseudoseizures was admitted after an episode of syncope associated with severe abdominal pain radiating to the left testicle, nausea, vomiting, and chest tightness. He had been unable to eat for three days and reported seeing blood and 'soot' in his vomit. In the ED, he had tachycardia and an elevated lactate of 7.2 with an anion gap of 24, which normalized after IV fluids. Workup ruled out myocardial infarction with normal troponins and EKG, and no arrhythmias on telemetry. The syncope was attributed to vagal episodes triggered by pain. He was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, pain control, and antiemetics. By hospital day two, his symptoms improved, he tolerated clear liquids, and was transitioned to oral medications. He was discharged home with improved pain, instructions to restart metformin, new prescription for ondansetron, and follow-up plans.
